source.title: The Hidden Risks of Large Reasoning Models: A Safety Assessment of R1
source.authors: Kai-Qing Zhou; Cheng-Zhi Liu; Xuandong Zhao; Shreedhar Jangam; Jayanth Srinivasa; Gao-Wen Liu; D. Song; X. Wang

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some figure and table content is flattened in the text extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial jailbreak and prompt-injection attacks can elicit harmful responses, using benchmark attack-success rates rather than the specific prefilling, suffix, or decoding interventions named in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study also compares safety rates for the reasoning-distilled R1-70b and Llama 3.3-70B, but this is not a controlled fine-tuning intervention and the paper does not characterize the distillation data as ordinary benign instruction data. Those comparative results are recorded as findings not covered by a claim version. It does not measure per-token KL, compliant prefilling, localized parameters, or safety deepening.
record.test_reason: The paper compares DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B with its safety-aligned starting model, Llama 3.3-70B, on the same unsafe-prompt benchmarks and attacks. This is a pre- versus post-fine-tuning comparison on reasoning-distillation data, a new setting bearing on V2. The authors frame it with Qi et al. (2023). It is uncontrolled: the authors did not run the fine-tuning, and they do not characterize the distillation data. The WildGuard jailbreaks are strategy-based natural-language prompts, not prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks, and there is no no-attack baseline, so they do not test V4. Prompt injection measures overriding of instructions, not harmful compliance.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that open reasoning models trail o3-mini on safety benchmarks and attacks. They say the distilled R1-70b 'compromises the original safety performance consistently in all the safety tests' relative to Llama 3.3. They also conclude that stronger reasoning makes unsafe answers more harmful, and that thinking traces carry hidden risks absent from final answers. Note that their own jailbreak table (R1-70b ASR 74.6 vs 82.1) contradicts the 'all safety tests' wording.
record.recipe_differences: Uses safety benchmark and adversarial-attack evaluations rather than few-example fine-tuning, token-position KL analysis, or targeted safety-depth interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Prompt-injection ASR differs by injection type and risk category; the authors state indirect-injection ASR is generally higher than direct-injection ASR and security-related ASR is higher than logic-related ASR.

fits_no_version.finding: WildGuard jailbreak ASR ranges 56.6-84.6 across seven models, with o3-mini lowest (Table 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Strategy-based natural-language jailbreaks succeed against both reasoning and non-reasoning models at high rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Prompt-injection ASR varies by injection type and risk category; open R1 models are more vulnerable than o3-mini (Table 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reasoning models remain susceptible to instruction-override prompt injection.

fits_no_version.finding: Thinking traces are less safe than final answers for R1-70b and R1 on all four datasets (Table 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety of a reasoning trace can lag behind safety of the final answer.

fits_no_version.finding: Unsafe responses of reasoning models score as more helpful to malicious queries (Fig 3, Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stronger reasoning increases the harmfulness of unsafe outputs.

record.problems: The model comparison does not isolate a causal training effect. The attack results have no reported uncertainty estimates. Safety judgments primarily use GPT-4o, though the appendix reports 96.7% accuracy against human labels on a sample of 240 responses from four models.
record.rows_left_out: Table 7 compares safety rates for reasoning text and final answers across AirBench, MITRE, Code Interp, and WildGuard. It was not retained because it does not measure the claim versions' token-position KL, compliant-opening bypass, or specified training interventions. Table 3's safe-prompt over-refusal results and Table 4's social-engineering/harmfulness scores do not measure the outcomes named by the versions. Figure-based examples were not separately rowed.

untested.parts: No controlled fine-tuning run, data composition, dose (number of examples) or benign-data selection. Only one checkpoint pair.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, adversarial-suffix or decoding attacks; jailbreaks are natural-language strategy prompts.
No test of data or objective causes. The authors speculate the distillation data may resemble harmful queries but do not test this.

missing.what: Per-category AirBench safety, R1-70b vs Llama3.3: mixed, worse in Operational Misuses and Security Risks, better in Hate/Toxicity
Code Interpreter per-category malicious rates: R1-70b worse than Llama3.3 in 4 of 5 categories (e.g. Social Engineering 77.0% vs 41.0%)
XSTest over-refusal: R1-70b full refusal 4.4% vs Llama3.3 2.4%

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 linkage is overturned: the jailbreaks are not opening-bypass attacks, and prompt injection is a different construct. V2 is linked via the R1-70b vs Llama3.3-70B checkpoint pair, with the caveat that it is not a controlled intervention. The judge is GPT-4o, reported at 96.7% agreement with human labels on 240 responses. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples is performed.
No ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning intervention is performed. The paper compares a reasoning-distilled model with a base counterpart, but does not isolate the effect of training.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL or response-position distribution is measured.
The study tests jailbreak and prompt-injection attacks, but not compliant-token prefilling, adversarial suffixes as a distinct intervention, or decoding changes.
No weight or rank localization is measured.
No data or training-objective cause of safety shallowness is tested.
No intervention intended to deepen safety across response tokens is evaluated.

relationships.condition: Unsafe-prompt benchmarks (AirBench, MITRE, Code Interpreter, Phishing): R1-70b vs its aligned Llama 3.3-70B base
relationships.reason: Safety rate is lower after reasoning distillation on all four benchmarks (C2, C4, C6, C8); Code Interp falls most, 70.4 to 43.2. Uncontrolled checkpoint comparison.
relationships.display_finding: Safety rates were lower after reasoning distillation on all four benchmarks, most on Code Interpreter (70.4 to 43.2), though the checkpoint comparison is uncontrolled.

relationships.reason: The distilled R1-70b has lower jailbreak ASR (74.6) than Llama3.3 (82.1), the reverse of eroded safety (J2, J3).
relationships.display_finding: Jailbreak ASR was 74.6 for R1-70b against 82.1 for Llama3.3, the reverse of eroded safety.

relationships.reason: From Figure 2 text, not rows: Llama3.3 beats R1-70b by >20% in Operational Misuses and Security Risks, but R1-70b is better on Hate/Toxicity by 11%.
relationships.display_finding: Llama3.3 beat R1-70b by more than 20% in Operational Misuses and Security Risks, but R1-70b was better on Hate/Toxicity by 11%.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: WildGuard jailbreak evaluation across the seven reported models
reader_labels.reason: Every model has a reported nonzero jailbreak ASR, ranging from 56.6 to 84.6; see J1–J7. This supports susceptibility to these attacks, not the specific prefilling, suffix, or decoding mechanisms.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: CyberSecEval prompt-injection evaluation across the seven reported models
reader_labels.reason: The aggregate ASR is nonzero for every model; the table also reports successful attacks under direct and indirect injection and both risk categories; see I1–I35.
